Package cliwerk.spec

Class CommandSpecDsl

java.lang.Object
cliwerk.spec.CommandSpecDsl
public final class CommandSpecDsl extends Object
A lightweight, human-friendly text format for describing a picocli CommandLine.Model.CommandSpec, as an alternative to hand-writing JSON. Compiling the DSL always produces the same CommandSpec model that CommandSpecJson reads and writes, so a spec can be authored in this DSL and exported to JSON for other tooling, or merged with other specs via CommandSpecMerger.

Grammar (informal)

 [ definitions {
     ( option <name> (, <name>)* : <type> ["<description>"] [default=<value>] [required] [arity=<range>]
     | positional <label> : <type> ["<description>"] [default=<value>] [required] [arity=<range>]
     )*
 } ]
 command <name> ["<description>"] {
     ( option <name> (, <name>)* ( : <type> ["<description>"] [default=<value>] [required] [arity=<range>] )?
     | positional <label> ( : <type> ["<description>"] [default=<value>] [required] [arity=<range>] )?
     | command ... (nested, same grammar)
     )*
 }

A positional parameter's bare &lt;label&gt; is wrapped as "&lt;label&gt;" to form its paramLabel, matching picocli's own convention for annotated fields. Supported &lt;type&gt; names are the same as CommandSpecJson's (currently scalar types only). A // starts a line comment, running to end of line; it is not recognized inside a quoted string.

A "&lt;description&gt;" may span several help lines: each \n inside it starts a new element of the resulting String[] description, and write(CommandSpec) joins multi-element descriptions back with \n, so descriptions survive a round trip unchanged.

An option/positional statement inside a command body that omits the : <type> part (and everything after it) is a reference to a same-named option or positional param declared once in the optional top-level definitions block, instead of a new definition -- the DSL's answer to many commands sharing the same option, without repeating its type/description/etc. verbatim in each one. A definition and a reference can be freely mixed within one command's own option/positional list. An option reference must name exactly one option (the one being referenced); a multi-name list only makes sense when defining (with a :), not referencing.

Example:

 definitions {
   option --release : boolean "Optimize for release"
 }
 command flix "The Flix programming language" {
   option -v, --verbose : boolean "Enable verbose output"
   command build "Compile the project" {
     option --release
   }
 }
